lesson.menu_title: Telling Personal Stories with a Backstory
lesson.menu_desc: Past perfect for the story before the story (had + past participle), story words and a reading about a missed flight -- reading model -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 32 — Telling Personal Stories with a Backstory
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 32 — Telling Personal Stories with a Backstory
lesson.grammar_point: past perfect for the backstory in narratives (had + past participle: the plane had already left)

listenings.text: Good storytellers do something simple. They do not tell everything in order. They start with the big moment, and then they go back. When I got to the gate, the plane had already left. In one sentence, you know two things: what happened, and what had happened before. That second part is the backstory, and English has a special form for it, had plus the past participle. I had forgotten. She had never seen the sea. We had already eaten. Try it the next time you tell a story. Start with the moment that surprised you. Then go back and explain. Your listener will stay with you, because now they want to know how it happened.

A few years ago, my wife and I drove three hours to a friend's wedding in the mountains. We were late, of course, because we had stopped twice for coffee. When we arrived, the ceremony had already started, so we sat quietly at the back. The bride was beautiful, but something was strange. I did not recognize anyone. Not one person. Then it dawned on me. We had come to the right church, but on the wrong day. Our friend's wedding was the next Saturday. We had walked into a stranger's wedding. Long story short, the family was very kind, they invited us to the party, and we danced until two in the morning. The next Saturday, we were the first guests to arrive.

extra_audio.text: First, I start with the big moment: when I got to the gate, the plane had already left. Then I go back in time: I had read the ticket wrong. After that, I say how I felt: I was stranded, and my phone was almost dead. Next, I tell the twist: out of the blue, a stranger offered to help. In the end, I give the lesson: long story short, it was a blessing in disguise.

reading.rtitle: The flight I missed in Lisbon
paras: Two years ago, I was on my way home from a work trip to Lisbon. I had planned everything. I had checked in online, I had packed the night before, and I had left the hotel three hours early. Or so I thought.

When I got to the airport, the departure board looked strange. My flight was not there. Then it dawned on me: I had read the ticket wrong. The flight had left at 10:15 in the morning, not at night. I was stranded in a city where I knew nobody, and my phone was almost dead.

I sat down and, to be honest, I almost cried. Out of the blue, a woman next to me asked if I was OK. She had missed her connection too. Meanwhile, the airline desk was looking for two seats on the next flight to Sao Paulo. We got them in the nick of time.
Long story short, we talked for ten hours on that plane, and today she is one of my closest friends. Missing that flight was a blessing in disguise. I still check my tickets three times, though.
reading.source: Personal blog post -- "The flight I missed in Lisbon"
